stories.headline: Four People Wounded in Harvey Park Shootout After Fight Escalates Overnight
stories.summary:
Four people were injured when a confrontation turned into a shootout shortly after 1 a.m. Saturday in Denver's Harvey Park neighborhood, according to Denver Police. The incident occurred in the 2100 block of South Sheridan Boulevard, with one victim transported by ambulance, one sustaining a minor gunshot wound to the foot, and two others driving themselves to a hospital.

Investigators believe the shooting began as an assault or physical fight involving an unknown number of participants. Detectives detained multiple people at the scene and recovered four firearms.

Anyone with information is asked to contact Metro Denver Crime Stoppers at 720-913-7867. The investigation is ongoing.

stories.headline: Flash Flooding Strands Motorists Across Denver South Metro, Rescuers Respond to Seven Incidents
stories.summary:
Severe thunderstorms swept through the Denver metro area Saturday afternoon, dropping heavy rain and substantial hail that triggered flash flooding across Douglas and Arapahoe counties. South Metro Fire Rescue responded to seven water rescue calls between 2:30 p.m. and 4 p.m., with stranded vehicles reported as far east as Parker Road.

At the intersection of Meridian Boulevard and Maroon Circle in Meridian, two to three feet of hail accumulated beneath standing water, creating an especially hazardous and deceptive condition. One driver, Kevin Plamondon, said his vehicle was lifted off the ground by the water before he escaped through his window. A separate incident was reported at Alameda Avenue and South Havana Street in Aurora, where at least three vehicles became stuck.

The Douglas County Sheriff's Office warned residents to avoid all areas with standing water and urged drivers never to attempt crossing flooded roadways. The Ken Caryl area in the southwest metro also reported significant hail accumulation. A severe thunderstorm watch remained in effect for much of the Front Range into the evening, with additional flooding possible in Northern Colorado.

stories.headline: Thirteen of Colorado's 25 Largest Communities Lack Mandatory Water Restrictions Despite Severe Drought
stories.summary:
Despite near-statewide drought conditions — rated severe, extreme or exceptional across much of the heavily populated Front Range — 13 of Colorado's 25 largest cities and towns have not implemented mandatory water use restrictions, according to a Denver Post analysis. The communities without additional mandatory rules, including Fort Collins, Pueblo and Boulder, are home to more than 1.5 million residents.

Water managers say the disparity reflects each provider's distinct portfolio of water rights, reservoir storage and supply sources rather than indifference to the drought. Denver Water and Aurora Water have both implemented mandatory restrictions, while Pueblo has neither mandatory nor voluntary rules in place. Boulder officials say existing storage levels do not require mandatory action this year, though they are monitoring reservoir levels closely.

Experts caution that while a single extreme drought year can be managed, consecutive dry years will stress even well-prepared systems. The winter's record-low snowpack has translated into anemic streamflows and drained reservoirs across the state.

stories.headline: Monsoon Pattern to Linger Through Sunday Before Denver Metro Dries Out Early Next Week
stories.summary:
Monsoon moisture will keep conditions unsettled across the Denver metro area through Sunday, with scattered showers and thunderstorms expected, particularly along the Palmer Divide. Storms Sunday are forecast to be slightly less widespread than Saturday's activity, though passing showers remain possible across much of the plains.

Conditions are expected to dry out and warm up Monday and Tuesday as high pressure builds, with temperatures climbing to around 90 degrees. A brief return of isolated to scattered storms is possible by Wednesday as a disturbance moves through the region, before high pressure re-establishes itself.

Temperatures are forecast to reach the low to mid 90s by the end of next week and into the following weekend.

stories.headline: Cherry Creek School District Spent More Than $500,000 Reimbursing Administrators' Pension Contributions
stories.summary:
Cherry Creek School District spent $504,759 last school year covering required pension contributions for a dozen top administrators — a benefit that most Colorado school districts surveyed by The Denver Gazette extend only to superintendents. The reimbursements, for contributions to the Public Employees' Retirement Association, exceeded those of any other district in the survey.

A Denver Gazette survey of 20 Colorado school districts found that 72 percent provide the PERA reimbursement in some form, but only Cherry Creek, Littleton and Poudre extend it to both the superintendent and executive staff. Denver Public Schools provides it to executive staff, though Superintendent Alex Marrero's contract does not include it; he instead receives a benefit tied to annual performance evaluations.

The practice comes as districts face tightening budgets and declining enrollment, which can reduce state funding tied to student counts. Cherry Creek also pays the federal and state income taxes associated with the reimbursements, an additional cost not widely replicated among surveyed districts.

stories.headline: Report: Denver's Government-Imposed Fees Add More Than $40,000 to Cost of New Home — Double Peer-City Average
stories.summary:
A new report from the Common Sense Institute finds that fees and taxes imposed by local government add more than $40,000 to the cost of a new 2,000-square-foot single-family home in Denver before construction begins — more than double the average policy-created cost across 12 peer cities in the Pacific Northwest, Midwest, Sunbelt and Southeast. The analysis identifies policy choices, rather than land scarcity, labor or materials costs, as a significant and underexamined driver of housing unaffordability.

The report argues that high construction-related government costs are undermining Colorado's economic competitiveness, making it harder for businesses to recruit and retain employees. Colorado has recently posted losses in both business establishments and domestic migration — trends the report links partly to housing costs.

The findings extend beyond Denver: some of the highest development charges identified in the study are found elsewhere along the Front Range, where much of the state's new single-family construction must occur. The report's authors contend that local policy decisions represent one of the few levers policymakers can directly control in addressing affordability.

stories.headline: Colorado Minimum Wage to Rise to $15.71 Statewide in 2027; Denver to Hit $19.84
stories.summary:
Colorado's statewide minimum wage will increase 55 cents to $15.71 on Jan. 1, 2027, the state labor department announced. Denver's minimum wage will rise 2.9 percent to $19.84, and the city of Edgewater — population 5,410 — will match Denver's rate after the Edgewater City Council approved an ordinance to align with the city rather than exceed it.

Boulder, which began paying above the state minimum in 2025, opted in July to take no action on its tipped minimum wage. Boulder County has planned a roughly 3 percent increase that would set its minimum at $17.32. New state laws passed since 2019 give local governments greater flexibility to set their own minimum wages, but those expansions are now prompting regular review as inflation and cost-of-living considerations shift.

Data cited in the Colorado Sun report show Denver's restaurant sector shed 6 percent of its jobs in 2025 compared with early 2020 levels, with full-service restaurant employment falling 15 percent over the same period — though economists debate how much of that decline is directly attributable to minimum wage increases versus other cost pressures including food prices, rent and post-pandemic demand shifts.

stories.headline: Ten Active Wildfires Burning Across Colorado, Covering More Than 163,000 Acres
stories.summary:
Ten named wildfires are currently burning across Colorado, collectively covering approximately 163,784 acres, according to the latest National Interagency Fire Center data. The largest active incidents include the Aspen Acres Fire in Custer County at 102,004 acres and 72 percent contained, the Gold Mountain Fire in Ouray County at 39,691 acres and 87 percent contained, and the Willow Fire in Lake County at 7,534 acres and 67 percent contained.

The fires are burning against a backdrop of severe to exceptional drought across the Front Range and mountains, following a winter of record-low snowpack. Dry soils, low humidity and heat have elevated fire risk across the state.

Fire officials remind residents that Front Range grass fires can ignite nearly year-round during Chinook wind events. Residents are urged to monitor official emergency channels and evacuation orders from local authorities.

stories.headline: Broncos' Davis Webb Draws Praise for Play-Calling Acumen in Preseason Win Over Falcons
stories.summary:
Denver Broncos offensive coordinator Davis Webb drew strong reviews for the efficiency and tempo of his play-calling in the team's 27-7 preseason victory over the Atlanta Falcons Friday night, with quarterback Sam Ehlinger and head coach Sean Payton both singling out Webb's smooth operation. The offense gained 217 yards and 14 first downs over its first four drives, opening the game with a six-play, 69-yard touchdown march.

Payton said Webb's quick play delivery allowed quarterbacks additional seconds to read defenses, and that the preseason was not being treated as an opportunity to conceal tendencies from future regular-season opponents. Second-year cornerback Jahdae Barron added a defensive score, returning an interception 98 yards for a touchdown late in the first half.

The Broncos finished with a 360-to-178 advantage in total yards and a plus-113 rushing differential. The preseason win extends Denver's exhibition winning streak to eight consecutive games over four seasons under Payton.

stories.headline: Rockies Win Third Straight as Zac Veen Homers in First Start Back From Triple-A
stories.summary:
The Colorado Rockies rallied for a 3-2 victory over the Arizona Diamondbacks, extending their winning streak to three games. Outfield prospect Zac Veen homered in his first start following a recall from Triple-A, providing a highlight in what has been a difficult season for the club.

The win offers a modest bright spot for a rebuilding Rockies franchise that has struggled for sustained success. Veen, widely regarded as one of the organization's top prospects, had been developing in the minor leagues before his latest call-up.

The Rockies' three-game winning streak represents one of their better recent stretches and gives the organization a positive data point as it evaluates young talent heading into the final weeks of the season.

stories.headline: Nuggets Decline Jalen Pickett's Team Option, Lower Asking Price on Peyton Watson Sign-and-Trade
stories.summary:
The Denver Nuggets have declined guard Jalen Pickett's team option, making him an unrestricted free agent, and have reduced their asking price in potential sign-and-trade discussions involving forward Peyton Watson. The moves signal roster reconfiguration efforts by the front office as the team prepares for the 2026-27 season.

Pickett appeared in limited minutes over his time with the Nuggets and had not secured a consistent role in the rotation. Watson, a former first-round pick, attracted trade interest but a deal has not yet been finalized at the lower asking price.

The decisions come shortly after the Nuggets' 2026-27 schedule was released, featuring 14 back-to-back games. Denver is expected to remain a Western Conference contender built around Nikola Jokic.

stories.headline: Colorado Confidential Informant Helped Kill Two Men After Plea Deal Freed Him, Records Show
stories.summary:
A Colorado man who received a plea deal that freed him from prison went on to assist in the killings of two people while serving as a confidential informant, according to records reviewed by a Colorado news outlet. The case raises questions about oversight of informant arrangements and the terms under which individuals with violent histories are released to cooperate with law enforcement.

The records detail how the informant was enlisted by authorities after his release and subsequently became involved in circumstances that led to two deaths. The full scope of law enforcement's knowledge of the informant's activities during that period is under scrutiny.

The case has drawn renewed attention to how confidential informant agreements are structured, monitored and terminated in Colorado, and whether adequate safeguards exist to prevent released informants from engaging in further violent conduct.

topStory.headline: Trump Approves Emergency Declaration for Indiana After Storms Kill 5, Trigger Major Flooding
topStory.summary:
President Donald Trump approved a Presidential Emergency Declaration for Indiana on Saturday, unlocking up to $5 million in federal assistance following severe storms that struck the state beginning August 11. The storms, which produced straight-line winds, tornadoes and widespread flooding, have been blamed for at least five deaths across Indiana.

The declaration came after a Saturday morning phone call between Trump and Indiana Gov. Mike Braun, who had already declared a statewide emergency. FEMA said the federal assistance will supplement state, tribal and local response efforts, covering costs for water rescues and evacuations, sandbagging and flood-fighting operations, emergency shelters and supplies, and medical transportation and debris clearing. Fifteen counties and multiple municipalities have also issued local disaster declarations, and Indiana's State Emergency Operations Center remains activated.

The storms brought winds of up to 99 mph in Gary and as much as 10 inches of rain in parts of central Indiana, with nearly a third of the state's counties reporting wind damage. Indianapolis experienced flooding not seen in more than 30 years, with the National Weather Service saying the event could approach a 100-year flood. The White River reached peak flood levels on the north side of Marion County Saturday evening, though engineers warned that peak levels would hold for several hours before receding and that floodwaters would continue moving downstream, with river gauges expected to peak near Raymond Street around 2 a.m. Sunday.

In the Rocky Ripple neighborhood of Indianapolis, hundreds of volunteers gathered at Hohlt Park to fill sandbags and reinforce levees, with reports of a breach on 54th Street Saturday evening. Town Councilor Megan Hulland said crews exhausted available sandbags, though more than 1,000 additional bags were reported to be en route from Shelby County. In Gary, power restoration efforts by NIPSCO were briefly halted after a worker's vehicle was struck by gunfire, though no injuries were reported; the utility said it expects 90 percent of affected customers to have power restored by Tuesday and full restoration by the following Friday.
